The question of whether beer helps with lactation in nursing mothers is genuinely contested in the evidence. On one hand, d2, d5, and d6 show that polysaccharides from barley and hops in beer may increase serum prolactin levels — with studies in non-lactating women finding beer raised prolactin by nearly 2.5-fold, and notably, a woman who drank nonalcoholic beer showed a comparable response [d6]. Animal studies also suggest a barley/malt polysaccharide is responsible for this prolactin increase [d6], and d3 cites a Munich study finding that barley polysaccharides stimulate prolactin and encourage milk production [d3].

On the other hand, d1, d2, and d5 make clear that alcohol itself does not increase milk production and can actively harm lactation: five or more drinks decrease milk letdown, and nursing after just 1–2 drinks can reduce the infant's milk intake by 20–23% and cause infant agitation and poor sleep [d2][d5]. The American Academy of Pediatrics does not recommend drinking alcohol while breastfeeding, and beer is not considered a true galactagogue [d1]. Only 42% of surveyed mothers who used beer as a galactagogue thought it actually increased milk supply [d2][d5].

Adding to the conflict, d4 notes that beer has been described as both an anti-galactagogue and, historically, a galactagogue, with a 19th-century physician recommending it for nursing mothers — directly contradicting modern assessments [d4]. The current scientific consensus, supported by high-credibility sources, is that any potential benefit comes from the non-alcoholic polysaccharide components (also present in non-alcoholic beer), while the alcohol itself is detrimental to milk production and infant health [d1][d2][d5][d6].
